cells.tense: Something is arriving now, and you are at the threshold to meet it with the pen in your hand.
cells.ask: Pick one piece of the build you've been keeping private and put it in front of another person this week. You still decide what happens to it after they've seen it.
cells.core:
Something is entering your life right now, and you're at the door to meet it. Not waiting for it to be finished, not bracing for it to go wrong, just standing where it comes in. You can feel what's forming and you're letting it form at its own speed.

What you're building is old enough to show someone, and quiet enough that nobody has had to look yet. The easy motion is to keep it private until it's undeniable. Not a rule: company can carry what solitude has been carrying alone. Put one visible piece of it in front of one person before the week ends, and stay in the room while they take it in. You can put it back under wraps tomorrow if you want; today it gets one witness.

cells.tense: You're already living past the arrival, bracing for the version of this that can't be written yet.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you've decided about how this build should go and set it down for a day. Let someone else's hands touch it in the meantime.
cells.core:
You're standing in the doorway already picturing the finished thing, and the picturing has opinions. The shape you've imagined, the way people will respond to it, the version where it works — you're arranging the future faster than it can arrive, and the speed is costing you the piece in front of you.

There's a difference between steering something new and forcing the ending. You can tell which one you're doing by how it feels when someone else reaches for it. Hand one part over without managing them while they hold it. If it comes back changed, that's information, not damage. Tomorrow you can take the lead again; today you'll see what it does without you.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already behind you, and you haven't turned around to look.
cells.ask: Go back and find the moment you first knew this thing could be real. Say out loud what that moment asked of you, then do one small thing it pointed to.
cells.core:
Something came to the door and you stayed where you were. Not laziness — the caution was reasonable, and standing still was the safer of the two moves at the time. So the arrival happened without you in it, and the new thing has been taking shape in the background, waiting for a hand it hasn't gotten.

What you know is still yours. The reason to make one small move now isn't that the chance is fresh; it's that the making still works on you after the timing has thinned. Find the first moment this thing looked real to you, hear what it asked for, and do one piece of that today. The force of it doesn't come from a mood.
cells.sheetLine: The moment passed, but what it asked for is still open.

cells.tense: You're already shaping what arrives and calling it the situation, with your hand still on the pen.
cells.ask: Pick one decision you've been calling obvious and say out loud that you chose it. Then stand behind it when someone questions you.
cells.core:
You've been treating this build like something that happens to you. It arrives, you respond, you call the response necessary — and all through it, the picking was yours. The version that got built, what you kept, which direction it took: you were the one deciding. That fact hasn't been given its due.

That's not a fault, it's a habit, and it costs you the traction that comes from claiming a direction. There's a moment when someone asks why it has to be this way, and you reach for precedent instead of preference. Next time, say you picked it. Stand behind it under real pressure, not in theory. If you want to change your mind after, you can — but own the first version first.
